newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel chief has fought Mobutu for decades.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel chief has fought Mobutu for decades.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila fought President Mobutu Sese Seko for more than 30 years before seizing most of Africa's third largest country in just seven months.
Kabila, who says his rebellion is not only about Zaire but about "changing the face of Africa", has insisted that in talks he will only discuss how Mobutu stands down.
He backs up his hard line by the lightning advance of his forces across Zaire and the fact that they now threaten the capital Kinshasa.
Many Mobutu supporters in the capital were riled in February by the sight of South Africa's President Nelson Mandela leaning on Kabila's arm in Johannesburg and addressing him as "General Kabila".

But in April he suffered his worst public relations defeat with international condemnation of treatment of Hutu Rwandan refugees. Characteristically, rebels responded by switching from denying access to aid workers to swamping them with refugees.
Kabila, 56, heads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL). Its cutting edge is Banyamulenge ethnic Tutsis who triggered the revolt in October.
"My long years of struggle were like spreading fertiliser on a field. But now it is time to harvest," the short, burly rebel leader told Reuters at his headquarters in eastern Zaire.
Known by supporters as Mzee, the Swahili word for Grand Old Man, Kabila is the public point man for his alliance of four obscure political groups which was only formed last October 8.

He says the parties to the alliance which met for the first time in Lemera, the first town to fall to the rebels, are his Popular Revolutionary Party (PRP), the National Council of Resistance for Democracy (NCRD), the Revolutionary Movement for the Liberation of Zaire (RMLZ) led by Masaso Minitaga Ndiaka, and the People's Democratic Alliance (PDA) led by Deo Bugera.

Analysts say a major asset for Kabila as the alliance leader is that he is not an ethnic Tutsi. Kinshasa still accuses him of being a puppet of the Banyamulenge, who have been denied citizenship, and ethnic brothers in Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi.
"The Banyamulenge wanted him for his experience and because he is not a Tutsi," said Gerard Prunier, a French specialist in the region. But he forged close links to Tutsis over the years.

Kabila dismisses Kinshasa's accusations he is a puppet. But the level of support the rebels received from numerous neighbouring countries as the war against Mobutu picked up fuelled widespread doubts about whether he calls the shots.
"I have lived with and known the Banyamulenge all my life. Many of them stood by me throughout my struggle against Mobutu's regime. The most important thing is that we are all Zaireans," he said.
Kabila is from mineral-rich Shaba in southern Zaire but has lived for many years among the Banyamulenge in the Mulenge Mountains south of Uvira, from where he plotted the uprising.
War in eastern Zaire began when the Banyamulenge, a community of roughly 400,000, resisted Zairean attempts to expel them to Rwanda, a land they left up to 200 years ago.
But its roots go deeper and the rebels have a solid spine of veterans who fought with Rwanda's Tutsis after 1990.
Like most of the Tutsi diaspora around the world, the Banyamulenge flocked to join the rebel group of Paul Kagame, now Rwanda's vice-president and military supremo.

Stocky with white-flecked hair, Kabila is a former comrade-in-arms of the late Argentine-born revolutionary leader Che Guevara, who was with Cuban guerrillas fighting in east Zaire in the early 1960s.

In 1965, Kabila joined a rebellion led by Pierre Mulele, an education minister in the government of Patrice Lumumba, in eastern Zaire when the former Belgian Congo narrowly avoided breakup just after independence.
Mobutu, president since 1965 but now ailing from cancer, crushed that rebellion with foreign help. Ironically some of the Banyamulenge herdsmen then fought alongside the Mobutu forces.
Kabila, who speaks perfect English despite coming from francophone Zaire, was a regular visitor to Uganda in the late 1980s after Yoweri Museveni's rebels took power in Kampala.

At the same time, exiled Rwandan Tutsis holding top positions in Museveni's army fine-tuned plans to invade their homeland. They did so in 1990 and won the war in 1994 after the radical Hutus in power had exterminated some 800,000 Tutsis.
The link from Museveni to Kagame to the Banyamulenge is at the heart of claims by Kinshasa and some African states that a plot is unfolding to create a "Tutsiland" in Central Africa.
But Kabila, as a non-Tutsi, says he is proof this is false.

He is married with six children and one of them, Joseph, is the alliance commander for the northern division which captured the northeastern capital of Kisangani and southeast mineral centre of Lubumbashi, Zaire's second largest city.
